items.title: Tim Ries interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 19, 2022
items.q: Henderson, Pepper Adams — all the people who came through Detroit — Hank Jones.

ctx.x: Yes, only in the sense of like I often would be the only white person within a few miles, not only of the club but like in the entire neighborhood. And I remember the first time I went, there was a famous trumpet player Marcus Belgrave who kind of was like helped oh like Kenny Garrett, Geri Allen, Robert Hurst, a lot of people played with him and he kind of like continued that lineage of like Donald Byrd and Yusef Lateef and Charles McPherson and all those amazing, you know Elvin and all those Detroit — Joe

Henderson, Pepper Adams — all the people who came through Detroit — Hank Jones. I mean I could go on, the list is so vast. So Marcus was like the guy when I was growing up. So I went and I had met Robert Hurst, Bob Hurst, the bass player and so he said, “Well you can come and sit in.” So I was there waiting my turn to sit in you know, I didn’t want to just like run up to the stage you know. So at the end of the set it was like the vibe was a little bit like I hadn’t met them and it was like you know, but it…

person maybe they work in an office with a black person but maybe they would never have gone and had a drink with that person or invited them to their house. Like are you actually friends with another person that doesn’t look like you? I don’t know. Maybe but probably not. It seems like it’s not — I hate to say white or black, but it’s not that simple but we just still haven’t — well here we are Russia is attacking. Why does war have to happen? And why does there have to be racial discrimination? Why does there…
